context_heading: How to judge a barrister for yourself
context: Barristers in England and Wales are regulated by the Bar Standards Board (BSB). You can check the Barristers' Register to see whether someone holds a current practising certificate and whether they are authorised to accept instructions directly from the public. In Scotland the equivalent professionals are advocates, regulated through the Faculty of Advocates.

Barristers usually work from chambers, with clerks who manage diaries and fees. Many can be instructed through a solicitor in the traditional way, and those registered under the Public Access scheme can be instructed directly by members of the public for suitable matters. When comparing, look at the barrister's specialism, how they can be instructed and what the fee covers.
tell_heading: What to tell iComply when enquiring
tell: Describe the legal issue or the type of hearing so we can match you with a barrister who specialises in it.
Say whether you want to instruct directly under the Public Access scheme or through a solicitor.
Give the location or court region where the matter is based, and say if you are willing to work with a barrister further away.
Explain whether you need representation at a hearing, written advice, or help drafting documents.
Mention any key dates or deadlines that the barrister should know about.
State that you are comparing barristers so we understand you are at the early stages of choosing.
questions_heading: Questions to ask a barrister you are comparing
questions: What is your specialist area of law and how much of your practice is in this field?
Are you authorised to accept instructions directly from the public under the Public Access scheme?
What is your approach to fees for a defined piece of work like mine?
How will you keep me informed about the progress of my case?
What do you need from me to give an initial view or quote?
Can you explain how the court or tribunal process will work for my situation?

faqs.q: How can I check that a barrister is regulated?
faqs.a: You can check the Barristers' Register on the Bar Standards Board's register to see whether someone holds a current practising certificate and whether they are authorised to accept instructions directly from the public.

faqs.q: What does Public Access mean for instructing a barrister?
faqs.a: Public Access allows members of the public to instruct a barrister directly for suitable matters, without going through a solicitor. Not all barristers are registered for it, so it is worth asking.

faqs.q: How are barristers' fees usually agreed?
faqs.a: Fees are usually agreed for a defined piece of work, so you should ask for a clear quote that sets out what is included. The clerk at the chambers can often explain this.

faqs.q: What should I compare when choosing a barrister?
faqs.a: Look at the barrister's specialism, whether they can accept direct instructions, their location and how their fees are structured. You can also ask about their experience in the type of hearing you face.

extra_heading: Comparing barristers when you want the best fit
extra: Searching for the best barrister comparison near me suggests you have already decided you want a barrister and are now working out how to weigh one against another. "Best" is personal here: the strongest choice for your matter is the one whose specialism matches your case, who can be instructed in the way you need, and whose fees you understand before you commit. No one can tell you who is best for you, but you can compare on those points yourself.

A true comparison is more than a list of names. Ask each barrister's chambers about their focus within the area of law your case involves, whether they accept direct instructions under the Public Access scheme, and how a quote for a defined piece of work would be structured. The clerk can usually answer these questions and explain what a fee covers, which makes side-by-side comparison far easier.

"Near me" is a sensible starting point, but it need not limit you. Much of a barrister's work is prepared in chambers and conducted at the court or tribunal hearing your matter, so a specialist further afield may suit you better than a generalist on your doorstep. Weigh location against specialism rather than treating distance as the deciding factor.

extra_faqs.q: Can I really compare barristers myself?
extra_faqs.a: Yes. You can look at each barrister's specialism, check their entry on the Barristers' Register, ask whether they accept direct instructions, and request a quote for your defined piece of work. Comparing those answers gives you a clearer picture than any single recommendation.

extra_faqs.q: Should I always choose the barrister closest to me?
extra_faqs.a: Not necessarily. Proximity can help with meetings, but the match between the barrister's specialism and your legal issue usually matters more. It is worth comparing a nearby barrister with a specialist further away before deciding.
